findings.title: Minimum token schema uses invalid computed object keys
findings.body: The minimum OAuth token schema uses computed keys like [z.string().toString()], which evaluate to a literal string key rather than creating a Zod record/catchall. This means the schema does not accept arbitrary OAuth token fields and will reject normal refreshed token responses when app credential sharing is enabled, causing token refresh failures across affected apps.

findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token can overwrite real refresh token
findings.body: If a refreshed token response does not include refresh_token, the code sets refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token". Callers that spread this parsed data into stored credentials, such as Office 365 and Zoom, can overwrite the real refresh token with this placeholder, permanently breaking future OAuth refreshes for that credential.

findings.title: App-specific token validation is bypassed whenever sync is enabled
findings.body: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, parseRefreshTokenResponse ignores the app-specific schema for every credential, even when refreshOAuthTokens falls back to the normal refresh path, such as for team credentials. This skips required app-specific validation and transforms, for example Office 365's expires_in conversion, and can store unusable credential keys.

findings.title: Google refresh assumes response.data but sync returns fetch Response
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response when credential sync is enabled, but GoogleCalendarService treats the result as a Google API response and accesses res?.data. In sync mode res.data is undefined, so accessing token.access_token throws and Google Calendar token refresh fails.

findings.title: Google stores Zod SafeParse result instead of parsed credential key
findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod SafeParse result, but GoogleCalendarService assigns that whole return value to key and saves it in credential.key. Subsequent credential reads will fail googleCredentialSchema.parse because the stored key is wrapped with success/data instead of containing the raw OAuth credentials.

findings.title: HubSpot treats sync fetch Response as parsed HubSpot token
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but HubspotCalendarService treats the return value as a parsed HubspotToken and reads expiresIn from it. This produces undefined/NaN expiry values and can store a Response-like object as the credential key, breaking HubSpot authentication.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin refresh expects Axios response data but sync returns fetch Response
findings.body: The normal Zoho Bigin refresh path returns an Axios response with a data property, but when credential sync is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response. The code then reads tokenInfo.data.error and mutates tokenInfo.data, which will throw or corrupt token handling for Zoho Bigin credentials.

findings.title: Zoho CRM refresh expects Axios response data but sync returns fetch Response
findings.body: The normal Zoho CRM refresh path returns an Axios response with a data property, but when credential sync is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response. The code then reads zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error and mutates zohoCrmTokenInfo.data, which will throw or corrupt token handling for Zoho CRM credentials.

findings.title: Salesforce uses prisma without importing it
findings.body: SalesforceCalendarService calls prisma.credential.update but does not import prisma. This will throw a ReferenceError at runtime whenever Salesforce credential refresh attempts to persist the new access token.

findings.title: Salesforce forces a token refresh on every client construction
findings.body: getClient performs an OAuth refresh-token request unconditionally, even if the stored access token is still valid. Because calendar service instances are created during normal event operations, this can generate excessive Salesforce token refresh requests, hit rate limits, and cause token rotation problems.

findings.title: Salesforce does not use the credential sync refresh path
findings.body: Unlike the other updated OAuth integrations, Salesforce refreshes directly against login.salesforce.com and never calls refreshOAuthTokens. When app credential sharing is enabled, Salesforce will not use CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT as the source of truth, defeating the purpose of the sync feature for this app.

findings.title: Zoom refresh sends incorrect app slug to sync endpoint
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens is called with appSlug "zoomvideo", but the Zoom credential/app identifier used elsewhere is "zoom". A self-hosted sync endpoint may fail to identify the app or refresh the wrong integration because the payload contains the wrong app slug.

findings.title: Credential sync helper returns raw response without a consistent contract
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT without checking response.ok or parsing JSON, while callers expect different shapes: some expect a parsed token object, some an Axios response, and some a fetch Response. This inconsistency causes runtime crashes or corrupted credential updates in several app adapters and hides sync endpoint errors.

findings.title: Webhook credential upsert is racy and can create duplicates
findings.body: The webhook handler performs findFirst followed by update or create without a transaction or unique constraint. Concurrent webhook calls for the same user/app can both find no existing credential and create duplicate credentials, leading to unpredictable app behavior and future updates only touching one duplicate.

findings.title: Credential sync update does not clear invalid flag
findings.body: When updating an existing credential, the webhook only writes key. If the credential was previously marked invalid, for example after an invalid_grant refresh failure, the newly synced valid credential remains marked invalid and may continue to be unusable.

findings.title: Webhook secret is compared with strict equality
findings.body: The webhook secret header is compared to CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET using !== instead of a constant-time comparison. For a secret-protected endpoint that can write OAuth credentials, a constant-time comparison is safer against timing-based secret leakage.
